subject: MATH
overview: Teach each day for about 60 minutes: a short fact-fluency warm-up, a modeled lesson with real objects (counters, base-ten blocks, rulers, coins), then guided and independent practice. Follow the concrete–pictorial–abstract path — let the child build it, draw it, then write it. Use Friday checks to decide what to reteach, and keep the fluency graph all year to celebrate growth. Always ask 'How do you know?' so the child explains strategies, not just answers.

weeks.prep: Gather a ten-frame (draw a 2×5 grid), 20 counters (beans or cereal), dot cards 1–10 (index cards with dots), two dice, and graph paper for the year-long fluency graph. Print or write a 40-fact quiz of sums and differences within 10.
misconceptions: Counting on from the first number instead of the larger one (2 + 8 counted as 3, 4, …, 10). Show that 8 + 2 = 2 + 8 with counters, then always start from the bigger number.
Starting the count on the number you already have (8 + 3 said as 8, 9, 10). Have the child put the 8 'in their head,' tap it, then say the NEXT numbers: 9, 10, 11.

days.guide: Flash a dot card or filled ten-frame for 2 seconds and ask 'How many? How did you see it?' Then fill a ten-frame with 7 counters and ask how many empty spaces (3) — that makes 7 + 3 = 10. The child writes all the facts that make 10, from 0 + 10 to 10 + 0, and looks for the pattern.

questions.q: What number goes with 6 to make 10?
questions.a: 4, because 6 + 4 = 10 (4 empty boxes on a ten-frame with 6 filled).

questions.q: Name all the pairs of numbers that make 10.

days.guide: Model 8 + 3: 'Put 8 in your head (tap your head), then count on 3 fingers: 9, 10, 11.' Show that 3 + 8 is easier if you start with 8. The child rolls two dice, counts on from the larger number, and writes 15 equations.

questions.q: Solve 3 + 9 by counting on.
questions.a: 12 — start at 9 (the larger number) and count on 3: 10, 11, 12.

questions.q: Solve 7 + 2.

days.guide: Show pictures for doubles (spider legs 4 + 4 = 8, egg carton 6 + 6 = 12, crayons 8 + 8 = 16). Say each double together, then quiz with flash cards; set aside any card that takes more than 3 seconds to practice again.

questions.q: What is 7 + 7?
What is 9 + 9? What is 5 + 5?

days.guide: Tell a take-away story ('You had 9 grapes and ate 4') while the child acts it out with counters and writes 9 − 4 = 5. Then ask 'What goes with 4 to make 9?' to connect it to 4 + 5 = 9. Do 5–6 stories.

questions.q: What is 9 − 4, and what addition fact helps?
There were 8 birds. 3 flew away. How many are left?

days.guide: Give the 40-fact quiz with a 2-minute timer; stop at the timer and count correct facts. Help the child color the first bar of the fluency graph. Then read 4 short stories aloud; the child draws and writes an equation for each.

questions.q: Lily has 6 stickers. She gets 3 more. How many now?
What is 10 − 7?

weeks.assessment_key: Fluency quiz: score = number correct out of 40; check each fact against an addition chart and graph the score (this is the baseline). Story problems (suggested): 1) Maya had 6 shells and found 3 more: 6 + 3 = 9 shells. 2) There were 10 ducks; 4 swam away: 10 − 4 = 6 ducks. 3) Ben has 5 cars and gets 2 more: 5 + 2 = 7 cars. 4) 8 cookies, 3 eaten: 8 − 3 = 5 cookies. Proficient = 34+ facts and 4/4 problems with a matching equation.

weeks.prep: Draw or print double ten-frames, gather 20 counters in two colors, and a deck of cards (remove face cards; Ace = 1). Make fact cards for 8 + and 9 + facts and near doubles.
misconceptions: Forgetting the leftover after making a ten (9 + 5 → 10 + 5 = 15). Have the child physically move 1 counter from the 5 to the 9 so they see 4 left: 10 + 4 = 14.
Adding 1 to the wrong double for near doubles (6 + 7 = 7 + 7 + 1). Say 'use the SMALLER double, then add 1': 6 + 6 + 1 = 13.

days.guide: Put 9 counters in the top ten-frame and 5 in the bottom. Ask 'How can we fill the top frame?' Move 1 counter up: now 10 + 4 = 14. Practice 8 + and 9 + facts the same way, saying the new equation aloud each time.

questions.q: Use make-a-ten to solve 9 + 6.
Use make-a-ten to solve 8 + 5.

days.guide: Show 6 + 7 with counters: 'I see a 6 + 6 double hiding, plus 1 more' — 12 + 1 = 13. The child explains a near double in their own words, then sorts 20 fact cards into piles: doubles, near doubles, make a ten, count on.

questions.q: Solve 7 + 8 with a near double.
Which strategy fits 9 + 4 best and what is the answer?

days.guide: Read each problem twice. The child underlines the question, draws circles or a quick sketch, and writes an equation with the answer labeled. Ask 'Are we putting together or taking apart?'

questions.q: Ana has 8 red and 7 blue marbles. How many marbles does she have?
There are 13 apples. 5 are green and the rest are red. How many are red?

days.guide: Make Ten Go Fish: ask for the card that makes 10 with one in your hand. Doubles War: each player flips a card and doubles it; the larger double wins. The child records 10 facts from each game on paper.

questions.q: In Make Ten Go Fish you hold a 3. What card do you ask for?
In Doubles War you flip an 8. What is your double?

days.guide: Give the 30-fact quiz, then read the 3 word problems aloud. Finish by asking the child to choose one fact and explain the strategy out loud while you listen for clear steps.

questions.q: Explain how to solve 8 + 6 with make-a-ten.
questions.a: Move 2 from the 6 to the 8 to make 10; 4 are left; 10 + 4 = 14.

questions.q: What is 6 + 5?

weeks.assessment_key: Fact quiz: 30 sums within 20, score out of 30 (proficient 25+). Suggested items include 9+5=14, 8+6=14, 7+8=15, 6+6=12, 9+7=16, 8+8=16, 5+7=12, 9+9=18, 8+4=12, 6+7=13. Word problems (suggested): 1) 8 red + 7 blue marbles = 15; 2) 12 cars, 9 are red, how many not red? 12 − 9 = 3; 3) 9 books + 6 books = 15. Strategy explanation: proficient if the child names a strategy and walks through it correctly (e.g., 'For 9 + 6 I moved 1 to the 9 to make 10, then 10 + 5 = 15').

weeks.prep: Make fact triangles (cut paper triangles; sum at the top corner, addends at the bottom corners), draw a 0–20 number line, and gather 20 counters. Write a 30-item subtraction fact quiz within 20.
misconceptions: Subtracting in the wrong order (writing 6 − 14). Use the fact triangle: the top number (the whole) always comes first in subtraction.
In compare problems, adding the two numbers because the problem says 'more.' Draw two bars lined up and ask 'how much extra does the longer bar have?'

days.guide: Show a fact triangle with 15 on top and 7, 8 on the bottom. Cover each corner and ask for the missing number. The child writes the 4 equations (7 + 8 = 15, 8 + 7 = 15, 15 − 7 = 8, 15 − 8 = 7) for 6 families.

questions.q: Write the fact family for 6, 9, and 15.
In a fact family, which number is the whole?
questions.a: The biggest number (the sum), e.g., 15 in 6, 9, 15.

days.guide: Model 14 − 6 by asking 'What goes with 6 to make 14?' Count up or recall 6 + 8 = 14, so 14 − 6 = 8. The child practices 20 subtraction cards, saying the related addition fact for each.

questions.q: Solve 14 − 6 by thinking addition.
Solve 17 − 9.

days.guide: On the 0–20 number line, start at 15 and jump back 5 to land on 10, then 2 more to land on 8 (5 + 2 = 7 jumps in all). Practice 6 problems, always stopping at 10 first.

questions.q: Solve 13 − 5 by going back through ten.
questions.a: 8 — back 3 to 10, then back 2 more to 8.

questions.q: Solve 12 − 4.

days.guide: Draw two bars: Leo's (13) longer than Mia's (8). Line them up and shade the extra part. Ask 'How many more?' and write 13 − 8 = 5 or 8 + 5 = 13. Do 5 similar problems.

questions.q: Leo has 13 stickers. Mia has 8. How many more does Leo have?
Sam read 11 books. Kai read 4 fewer than Sam. How many did Kai read?

days.guide: Give the 30-fact subtraction quiz, then the 4 mixed word problems. The child must show a drawing (circles or bar model) and an equation for each.

questions.q: There were 16 grapes. Tom ate some. Now there are 9. How many did he eat?
What is 11 − 3?

weeks.assessment_key: Subtraction quiz: 30 facts within 20, score out of 30 (proficient 25+). Suggested items: 14−6=8, 15−7=8, 13−9=4, 12−5=7, 16−8=8, 11−4=7, 17−9=8, 18−9=9, 12−8=4, 15−6=9. Word problems (suggested): 1) Leo has 13 stickers, Mia has 8: 13 − 8 = 5 more. 2) 15 birds, 7 fly away: 8 left. 3) Jen has 9 beads and needs 16: 16 − 9 = 7 more. 4) 6 red + 9 blue = 15 balloons. Each needs a drawing and correct equation.

weeks.prep: Draw bar-model mats (a long rectangle split into two parts), gather counters and a timer, and have the Week 1 fluency graph ready. Prepare a 40-fact quiz within 20 and 6 word problems.
misconceptions: Thinking the box always holds the answer at the end; for 8 + □ = 15 the child writes 23. Read it as 'eight plus what makes fifteen?' and use counters to count up from 8.
In start-unknown problems, adding the numbers (6 + 14 = 20). Draw the bar: the whole is 14, one part is 6, find the other part: 14 − 6 = 8.

days.guide: Write 8 + □ = 15. Put out 8 counters, then add counters one at a time until there are 15 — count how many you added (7). Repeat with □ − 4 = 9 by asking 'What number, take away 4, leaves 9?' (13).

questions.q: Solve 8 + □ = 15.
Solve □ − 4 = 9.

days.guide: Read the bird story and draw a bar: total 14, known part 6, unknown part '?' at the start. Ask 'Do we know the whole? Which part is missing?' Solve 14 − 6 = 8, then check: 8 + 6 = 14. Solve 5 like it.

questions.q: Some birds were on a tree. 6 more came. Now there are 14. How many were there at first?
Some kids were at the park. 5 went home. Now 7 are there. How many were there at first?

days.guide: Help the child write three stories with the same numbers, moving the unknown: end (5 + 4 = ?), middle (5 + ? = 9), start (? + 4 = 9). A family member solves them and the child checks with the equation.

questions.q: Write an equation for: 'I had some cars. I got 4 more. Now I have 9.'
Which part is unknown in 'Max had 10 pens and lost some. Now he has 6'?

days.guide: Set three stations for about 10 minutes each: fact-triangle flash, 'Salute!' (two players hold a card to their foreheads without looking; a caller says the sum; each player figures out their own card), and an online fact practice session. Note facts that are still slow.

questions.q: In Salute!, the sum is 13 and you see your partner's 6. What is your card?
What is 9 + 8?

days.guide: Give the 40-fact quiz with the timer and graph the score beside the baseline. Then read the 6 word problems; the child writes an equation with a box for each before solving.

questions.q: Mia had 15 beads. She gave some to a friend. Now she has 9. How many did she give away?
Some apples were in a bowl. Dad added 5. Now there are 12. How many at first?

weeks.assessment_key: Fluency quiz: score out of 40; add the new bar to the Week 1 graph and compare (growth is the goal). Word problems (suggested): 1) 7 + □ = 15 → 8. 2) □ − 4 = 9 → 13. 3) Some birds were on a tree, 6 more came, now 14 → 8 birds. 4) 12 crayons, gave some away, 5 left → 7 given away. 5) Ana has 9 shells, Ben has 4 more than Ana → 13. 6) 18 cookies, 9 eaten → 9 left. Proficient: 5–6 correct with matching equations.

weeks.prep: Gather base-ten blocks (or cut paper: 1×1 squares, 1×10 strips, 10×10 flats), about 100 straws and rubber bands, and draw a place-value mat (hundreds | tens | ones). Learn quick pictures: square = hundred, line = ten, dot = one.
misconceptions: Reading 305 as 'thirty-five' or writing 'three hundred five' as 3005. Build it with blocks and point out the empty tens column — the 0 holds that place.
Thinking the digit 4 in 346 is worth 4. Ask 'What does the 4 stand for?' and show 4 ten-rods = 40.

days.guide: Count out 10 straws and bundle with a rubber band — 'one ten.' Make 10 bundles, then bundle those into one big bundle — 'one hundred.' The child counts the tens by 10s to 100 and says why 100 = 10 tens.

questions.q: How many tens are in 100?
How many ones are in 3 tens?

days.guide: Say a number (346); the child builds it with 3 flats, 4 rods, 6 units on the mat, says 'three hundreds, four tens, six ones,' and draws a quick picture. Repeat for 10 numbers.

questions.q: What blocks show 346?
Draw 218 as a quick picture.

days.guide: Build 305, 350, and 503 side by side. Ask what the zero means in each (no tens; no ones; no tens). Have the child read each aloud correctly and tell which is greatest.

questions.q: What does the 0 in 305 mean?
questions.a: There are no tens — 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 5 ones.

questions.q: Which is greatest: 305, 350, or 503?

days.guide: Count flats by 100s to 900. Then show 4 flats and ask how many rods would cover them (40) and how many units (400). The child completes: 4 hundreds = __ tens = __ ones.

questions.q: 4 hundreds = how many tens = how many ones?
How many hundreds are in 700?

days.guide: Give the quiz: the child writes the number for 8 block pictures and the value of an underlined digit in 8 numbers. Have them build any missed item with blocks to self-correct.

questions.q: What is the value of the 7 in 175?
What number is 6 flats, 2 rods, 9 units?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested): block pictures — 1) 2 flats, 3 rods, 5 units = 235 2) 4 flats, 0 rods, 7 units = 407 3) 1 flat, 5 rods = 150 4) 6 flats, 2 rods, 9 units = 629 5) 3 flats, 8 units = 308 6) 9 flats, 9 rods, 9 units = 999 7) 5 flats, 1 rod, 1 unit = 511 8) 7 flats, 4 rods, 2 units = 742. Underlined digit values: 9) the 4 in 346 = 40 10) the 3 in 346 = 300 11) the 8 in 812 = 800 12) the 0 in 506 = 0 13) the 7 in 175 = 70 14) the 2 in 932 = 2 15) the 6 in 460 = 60 16) the 5 in 581 = 500. Proficient: 14/16.

weeks.prep: Print a hundreds chart and blank chart sections (or draw grids), and collect about 20 nickels and 20 dimes. Write 6 skip-count patterns and 10 '10/100 more or less' problems for Friday.
misconceptions: Counting correctly to 100 but stumbling across later hundreds ('198, 199, 1000'). Use blocks: 10 tens trade for the next hundred, so 199 + 1 = 200.
Changing the wrong digit when adding 10 (456 + 10 = 556). Ask 'Which digit is in the tens place?' and add one rod.

days.guide: Count aloud together from 87 to 132 while the child fills a blank chart section, then 385 to 421. Stop at 99→100 and 399→400 and ask what changed (the hundreds digit goes up; tens and ones become 0).

questions.q: What number comes after 199?
Count on from 397: what are the next 4 numbers?

days.guide: Lay out nickels and count by 5s; lay out dimes and count by 10s. Then start at 23 on the hundreds chart and jump down by 10s: 23, 33, 43 — only the tens digit changes.

questions.q: Skip-count by 10s from 23 to 73.
How much are 7 nickels?

days.guide: Skip-count by 100s from 100 to 1,000, then from 250 (250, 350, 450…). Draw a number path and show 10 more/less and 100 more/less for a number like 460 (470, 450, 560, 360).

questions.q: Skip-count by 100s from 250 to 750.
What is 100 less than 460? 10 more?

days.guide: Do 20 quick oral problems: add or subtract 10 or 100 from numbers 100–900. After each, ask which digit changed. Watch for crossing a hundred (395 + 10 = 405).

questions.a: 692 (there are 0 tens, so 70 tens − 1 ten = 69 tens, and 2 ones stay).

days.guide: The child fills in 6 skip-count patterns and solves 10 more/less problems. Review any errors with blocks or the number path.

questions.q: What is 10 more than 390?

weeks.prep: Make place-value arrow cards (hundreds 100–900, tens 10–90, ones 1–9 on strips that stack), and write a number-word list (one–nineteen, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, hundred).
misconceptions: Writing expanded form as 4 + 2 + 7 for 427. Use arrow cards to show the 4 is really 400 and the 2 is really 20.
Writing 'six hundred thirty-two' as 600302. Stack arrow cards 600, 30, and 2 so they overlap into 632.
Spelling 'forty' as 'fourty.' Point out forty has no u, while four and fourteen do.

days.guide: Lay arrow cards 400, 20, and 7 side by side, then stack them so they show 427. The child writes 427 = 400 + 20 + 7 and does 10 more numbers.

questions.q: Write 538 in expanded form.
Write 604 in expanded form.

days.guide: Practice spelling tricky number words (twenty, forty, ninety, hundred). Model writing 632 as 'six hundred thirty-two' — a hyphen joins the tens and ones words. The child writes 8 numbers in words.

questions.q: Write 632 in words.
Write 450 in words.

days.guide: Show 245 four ways: blocks, quick picture, expanded form (200 + 40 + 5), and 24 tens 5 ones (trade each hundred for 10 tens). Ask why 24 tens and 2 hundreds 4 tens are the same amount.

questions.q: Show 245 as tens and ones.
questions.a: 24 tens and 5 ones (2 hundreds = 20 tens, plus 4 tens = 24 tens).

questions.q: How many tens are in 360?

days.guide: Read riddles aloud and let the child build the answer: 'I have 3 hundreds, 0 tens, and 9 ones' (309). The child writes 3 riddles for a family member and checks the answers.

questions.q: I have 3 hundreds, 0 tens, and 9 ones. What number am I?
I have 7 ones, 5 hundreds, and 2 tens. What number am I?

days.guide: Give the 12-item conversion quiz. The child reads each item aloud first. Have them build any missed number with arrow cards to fix it.

questions.q: Write 'nine hundred fifty-six' in standard form.
Write 173 in expanded form.

weeks.assessment_key: Form-conversion quiz (suggested 12 items with answers): 1) 427 → 400 + 20 + 7 2) 815 → eight hundred fifteen 3) 300 + 60 + 2 → 362 4) five hundred nine → 509 5) 740 → 700 + 40 6) nine hundred ninety → 990 7) 200 + 8 → 208 8) 631 → six hundred thirty-one 9) four hundred forty-four → 400 + 40 + 4 10) 100 + 70 + 3 → 173 11) 956 → nine hundred fifty-six 12) seven hundred twenty → 720. Proficient: 10/12 (minor spelling errors OK if the number is right).

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks and digit cards 0–9 (two sets). For Wednesday, look up two or three landmark heights in feet or town populations under 1,000 (or use family heights in inches). Prepare the 20-item Unit 2 test.
misconceptions: Comparing by the ones digit first (thinking 329 > 412 because 9 > 2). Always compare hundreds first, then tens, then ones.
Mixing up > and <. Teach 'the open mouth faces the bigger number' and have the child read the sentence aloud ('452 is greater than 425').

days.guide: Build 452 and 425 with blocks. Compare hundreds (both 4), then tens (5 tens > 2 tens), so 452 > 425. The child records with a symbol and reads it aloud.

questions.q: Compare 452 and 425.
questions.a: 452 > 425; same hundreds, but 5 tens is more than 2 tens.

questions.q: Compare 610 and 601.
questions.a: 610 > 601; same hundreds, and 1 ten is more than 0 tens.

days.guide: The child compares 15 pairs with >, =, < and writes one explanation sentence. Check that the sentence names the place that decides it.

questions.q: Compare 362 and 326 and explain.
questions.a: 362 > 326 because 6 tens is more than 2 tens (the hundreds are equal).

questions.q: Compare 198 and 201.
questions.a: 198 < 201 because 1 hundred is less than 2 hundreds.

days.guide: Write 4 numbers on cards; the child orders them least to greatest by sorting on hundreds first, then tens. Then order the real numbers you looked up.

questions.q: Order 532, 253, 325, 523 from least to greatest.
Which is tallest: a 305-foot tower, a 350-foot tower, or a 299-foot tower?

days.guide: Each player draws 3 digit cards and makes the greatest and least numbers possible; the greater number wins the round. Play 10 rounds and record each comparison with a symbol.

questions.q: Make the greatest and least numbers with 4, 7, 1.
With 0, 5, 3, what is the least three-digit number?
questions.a: 305 (0 cannot go in the hundreds place).

days.guide: Give the 20-item Unit 2 test independently. Read directions aloud if needed, but not the answers. Afterward, reteach any missed place with blocks.

questions.q: What is 100 more than 285?
Compare 845 and 799.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test (suggested 20 items with answers): 1) 3 flats, 4 rods, 2 units = 342 2) value of 6 in 567 = 60 3) 100 more than 285 = 385 4) 10 less than 400 = 390 5) skip by 5s: 35, 40, 45, 50 6) skip by 100s: 120, 220, 320, 420 7) 700 + 50 + 9 = 759 8) 806 in words = eight hundred six 9) two hundred thirteen = 213 10) 914 expanded = 900 + 10 + 4 11) 452 > 425 12) 309 < 390 13) 671 = 671 14) 198 < 201 15) 845 > 799 16) order 532, 253, 325, 523 least to greatest → 253, 325, 523, 532 17) 18 tens = 180 18) count on: 398, 399, 400, 401 19) greatest number with 4, 7, 1 = 741 20) least = 147. Proficient: 17/20.

weeks.prep: Gather a 12-inch ruler, yardstick, measuring tape, and a box of same-size paper clips. Choose 10 household objects to measure (pencil, spoon, shoe, book). For Friday, draw 6 lines or objects of exact whole-inch lengths.
misconceptions: Starting at the 1 instead of 0 (or at the very end of the ruler). Put a finger on the 0 mark and line the object up there, or count the spaces, not the marks.
Leaving gaps or overlapping units. Show that gaps make the count too small and overlaps make it too big.

days.guide: Measure a book with paper clips left with gaps, then overlapping, then end-to-end. Compare the three counts and ask which is right and why. Conclude: same-size units, no gaps, no overlaps.

questions.q: Why do we line up paper clips with no gaps?
questions.a: Gaps leave parts unmeasured, so the count would be too small.

questions.q: If clips overlap, is the count too big or too small?
questions.a: Too big — some length gets counted twice.

days.guide: Show the 0 mark on the ruler. Line up a pencil at 0 and read the nearest inch. The child measures 10 objects and records them in a two-column table (object | inches).

questions.q: A crayon ends just past the 3-inch mark. To the nearest inch, how long is it?
Where do you line up the end of the object?
questions.a: At the 0 mark (the start) of the ruler.

days.guide: Show that 12 inches = 1 foot (a ruler) and 3 feet = 1 yard (a yardstick). Measure a table, a door, and a room; the child picks the tool and says why (tape for long or curved things).

questions.q: Which tool is best for measuring a room?
questions.a: A measuring tape or yardstick — it is long.

questions.q: How many inches are in 1 foot?

days.guide: The child estimates, then measures 8 objects, recording both. Find the difference between estimate and measurement and celebrate estimates within 2 inches.

questions.q: You estimated 6 inches and measured 9 inches. How far off were you?
Would you measure a shoe in inches or feet?
questions.a: Inches — it is shorter than a foot.

days.guide: Give the measuring check and the unit/tool quiz. Watch the child's ruler placement on each item and correct the starting point on the spot.

questions.q: What unit and tool would you use for the height of a door?
questions.a: Feet; a measuring tape or yardstick.

questions.q: What unit and tool for the length of a spoon?

weeks.assessment_key: Measuring check: prepare 6 pictured lines of known length (e.g., 3 in, 5 in, 2 in, 6 in, 4 in, 7 in); accept the exact whole inch. Unit/tool choice (suggested): 1) length of a pencil → inches, ruler 2) length of a room → feet, measuring tape or yardstick 3) height of a door → feet, tape or yardstick 4) length of a crayon → inches, ruler 5) length of a car → feet, measuring tape 6) width of a book → inches, ruler. Proficient: 5/6 measurements correct and 5/6 unit choices.

weeks.prep: Get a centimeter ruler, a meter stick (or cut string exactly 100 cm long), and sticky notes. Benchmarks: the width of a fingertip is about 1 cm; a giant step is about 1 meter.
misconceptions: Thinking an object got longer because the number in centimeters is bigger. Measure the same pencil in inches and cm: the pencil didn't change — smaller units need more of them.
Reading the inch side of a ruler by mistake. Label the cm side with a sticky note.

days.guide: Show that a fingertip is about 1 cm wide. The child measures 10 small objects (eraser, crayon, coin) to the nearest centimeter, starting at 0, and records them.

questions.q: A paper clip measures between 3 and 4 cm but closer to 3. What do you record?
What part of your body is about 1 cm?

days.guide: Walk with giant steps (about 1 meter each) to estimate a room's length, then measure with the meter stick, marking each meter with a sticky note. Compare estimate and measurement.

questions.q: How many centimeters are in 1 meter?
Would you measure a hallway in cm or m?

days.guide: Measure 5 objects in inches and in centimeters. Ask 'Why is the cm number bigger?' Guide to: a centimeter is a smaller unit, so it takes more of them.

questions.q: A book is 10 inches long. Will its length in centimeters be more or less than 10?
questions.a: More than 10 (about 25 cm), because centimeters are smaller units.

questions.q: Which is longer: 1 inch or 1 centimeter?

days.guide: Estimate 8 lengths using benchmarks (fingertip = 1 cm, giant step = 1 m), then measure. Color estimates that were within 5 cm.

questions.q: You estimated 30 cm and measured 34 cm. Was it within 5 cm?
Estimate a door's height: about 2 cm, 2 m, or 20 m?

days.guide: Give the metric quiz and have the child write one sentence explaining unit size. Check for the word 'smaller' and the idea of 'more units.'

questions.q: Explain why you get a bigger number in centimeters than in inches.
questions.a: Centimeters are smaller units, so more of them fit along the same length.

questions.q: A line starts at 0 and ends at the 7 cm mark. How long is it?

weeks.assessment_key: Metric quiz (suggested): measure 4 drawn lines of 5 cm, 8 cm, 12 cm, 3 cm (accept exact or ±1 cm). Compare inch vs. cm for 3 objects — the cm number must be larger each time (about 2½ times the inches). Unit-size sentence rubric: 3 = 'A centimeter is smaller than an inch, so it takes more centimeters to measure the same object'; 2 = says the cm number is bigger without the reason; 1 = incorrect relationship.

weeks.prep: Rulers (inch and cm), ribbon or string, scissors, a toy car and a board or large book for a ramp, and masking tape to mark start lines. Prepare Unit 3 test objects and 4 word problems.
misconceptions: Adding the two lengths to find 'how much longer.' Lay the objects side by side and point to only the extra part — subtract or count up.
Comparing measurements in different units (8 inches vs. 15 cm). You can only compare when both are in the same unit.

days.guide: Measure two pencils (e.g., 7 in and 4 in) and lay them side by side at a starting line. Count on from the shorter length to the longer: 5, 6, 7 — 3 inches longer. Write 7 − 4 = 3.

questions.q: Pencil A is 7 inches and pencil B is 4 inches. How much longer is A?
A crayon is 9 cm and a marker is 14 cm. How much longer is the marker?

days.guide: Cut 4–5 ribbons of different lengths. The child measures each in cm and writes 5 sentences: 'The red ribbon is __ cm longer than the blue ribbon,' with the subtraction shown.

questions.q: A red ribbon is 25 cm and a blue ribbon is 16 cm. How much longer is the red one?
What operation finds 'how much longer'?
questions.a: Subtraction (or counting up from the shorter to the longer).

days.guide: Set up a ramp and roll a toy car 5 times from the same start, marking where it stops. Measure each distance in inches, find the farthest and shortest, and subtract to find the difference.

questions.q: The farthest roll was 48 inches and the shortest was 30. What is the difference?
Why must every roll start at the same line?
questions.a: So the measurements are fair to compare.

days.guide: Measure arm spans (fingertip to fingertip, arms stretched wide) of family members in inches. The child writes compare sentences using subtraction.

questions.q: Dad's arm span is 66 inches and yours is 48. How much longer is Dad's?
Mom's span is 62 inches, yours is 48. How much longer?

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test: measure objects in two units, estimate lengths, and solve 4 'how much longer' problems with equations.

questions.q: For the same object, will the number be bigger in inches or in centimeters?
questions.a: Centimeters, because they are smaller units.

questions.q: A rope is 35 inches and a string is 20 inches. How much longer is the rope?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test (suggested): measuring — 3 objects measured in inches and cm (accept ±1 unit; the cm number should always be larger). Estimates — reasonable choices (e.g., a door about 7 feet or 2 meters; a pencil about 7 inches or 18 cm). Problems: 1) Pencil A 7 in, pencil B 4 in: 3 in longer. 2) Ribbons 25 cm and 16 cm: 9 cm longer. 3) Car rolled 48 in and 30 in: 18 in farther. 4) Dad's arm span 66 in, child's 48 in: 18 in longer. Proficient: accurate measures and 3/4 problems with equations.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks, a printed hundreds chart, and paper for open number lines (a blank line with no numbers). Write 12 practice problems for Friday (mix with and without regrouping).
misconceptions: Writing each column's sum side by side without regrouping (47 + 36 = 713). Build both numbers with blocks and trade 10 ones for a ten: 83.
On the hundreds chart, moving right for tens instead of down. Remind: down one row = +10, right one square = +1.

days.guide: Build 34 and 25 with blocks. Push the tens together (3 + 2 = 5 tens), then the ones (4 + 5 = 9): 59. The child solves 10 problems without regrouping, building or drawing each.
On a hundreds chart, put a finger on 46. Jump down 2 rows (+20) to 66, then right 3 (+3) to 69. Ask why going down a row adds 10.

questions.q: Use the hundreds chart for 46 + 23.
Why does moving down one row add 10?
questions.a: Each row has 10 numbers, so the number below is 10 more.

days.guide: Draw an open number line. Start at 38, jump +20 to 58, +2 to 60, +5 to 65. The child solves 8 more, labeling each jump.

questions.q: Solve 38 + 27 on an open number line.
Solve 45 + 36 on a number line.

days.guide: Build 47 + 36: 7 + 6 = 13 ones — trade 10 ones for a ten. Now 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 tens and 3 ones = 83. The child draws quick pictures for 8 regrouping problems, circling the 10 ones they trade.

questions.q: 47 + 36 = ? Explain the trade.
questions.a: 83 — 13 ones become 1 ten and 3 ones, so 8 tens 3 ones.

days.guide: Give the 12-problem quiz; the child may choose any strategy. Then they write how they solved one problem in 2–3 sentences.

questions.q: Explain 25 + 48.

weeks.assessment_key: Addition quiz (suggested 12): 1) 34 + 25 = 59 2) 46 + 23 = 69 3) 38 + 27 = 65 4) 47 + 36 = 83 5) 52 + 41 = 93 6) 29 + 18 = 47 7) 63 + 28 = 91 8) 15 + 75 = 90 9) 44 + 44 = 88 10) 56 + 37 = 93 11) 71 + 19 = 90 12) 25 + 48 = 73. Written explanation rubric: 3 = names a strategy and shows each step with correct place-value words (e.g., '38 + 27: 38 + 20 = 58, + 2 = 60, + 5 = 65'); 2 = correct steps, vague words; 1 = answer only. Proficient: 10/12 and a level-3 explanation.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks and open number line paper. Write 12 quiz problems for Friday (about half need decomposing a ten).
misconceptions: Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column (52 − 17 = 45). Build 52 and show you can't take 7 ones from 2 ones — trade a ten first: 35.
Counting up but forgetting to add the jumps together at the end. Circle each jump and add them.

days.guide: Build 68 and take away 2 tens and 5 ones to leave 43. The child draws quick pictures and crosses out what is taken away for 10 problems without regrouping.
Build 52. Try to take 7 ones from 2 — not enough. Trade 1 ten for 10 ones (now 4 tens 12 ones). Take 7 ones (5 left) and 1 ten (3 tens left): 35. The child solves 8 problems with drawings.

questions.q: Why do we trade a ten in 61 − 24?
questions.a: There is only 1 one, not enough to take away 4, so trade 1 ten for 10 ones (5 tens 11 ones); 61 − 24 = 37.

days.guide: Solve 83 − 48 by counting up on a number line: 48 → 50 (+2), 50 → 80 (+30), 80 → 83 (+3): 2 + 30 + 3 = 35. Compare with take-away using blocks — same answer.

questions.q: Solve 83 − 48 by counting up.
Solve 70 − 46 by counting up.

days.guide: The child solves 10 subtraction problems, then checks each by adding the answer to the number taken away. Ask why it works: the two parts make the whole.

questions.q: Check 74 − 29 = 45 with addition.
Why does addition check subtraction?
questions.a: The answer plus the part taken away must put the whole back together.

days.guide: Give the 12-problem quiz and ask for one written strategy explanation using the words tens, ones, and trade.

weeks.assessment_key: Subtraction quiz (suggested 12): 1) 68 − 25 = 43 2) 52 − 17 = 35 3) 83 − 48 = 35 4) 90 − 36 = 54 5) 74 − 29 = 45 6) 57 − 34 = 23 7) 61 − 24 = 37 8) 45 − 18 = 27 9) 80 − 47 = 33 10) 96 − 52 = 44 11) 73 − 38 = 35 12) 100 − 64 = 36. Explanation rubric: 3 = strategy with correct place-value steps; 2 = correct but vague; 1 = answer only. Proficient: 10/12.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks and a grocery store flyer (or make price tags under $1). Write 8 multi-addend problems for Friday.
misconceptions: Losing track of numbers when adding 3–4 addends. Teach crossing off each number as it is used.
Forgetting regrouped tens when the ones total is more than 20 (e.g., 24 ones = 2 tens 4 ones). Build the ones with blocks to see.

days.guide: Write 23 + 15 + 17. Ask 'Which two make a friendly number?' (23 + 17 = 40), then add 15: 55. The child solves 8 problems, circling the pair added first.
Add 24 + 31 + 12 + 18 by tens (20 + 30 + 10 + 10 = 70) then ones (4 + 1 + 2 + 8 = 15), then 70 + 15 = 85. Check with blocks.
Add 35 + 26 + 15 in three different orders and compare: always 76. The child explains in their own words that the order doesn't change the sum.

questions.q: Add 35 + 26 + 15 in two orders.
Does 8 + 7 equal 7 + 8? Why?
questions.a: Yes, both are 15 — you can add in any order.

days.guide: Pick 3–4 items under $1 from the flyer, write prices in cents, and add. Check whether the total is under or over $1 (100¢).

questions.q: Is 35¢ + 40¢ + 30¢ more or less than $1?

days.guide: Give 8 multi-addend problems; for two, the child writes which numbers were grouped first and why.

questions.q: Which pair would you add first in 37 + 13 + 40? Why?

weeks.assessment_key: Multi-addend quiz (suggested 8): 1) 23 + 15 + 17 = 55 2) 24 + 31 + 12 + 18 = 85 3) 35 + 26 + 15 = 76 4) 45 + 29 + 18 = 92 5) 16 + 14 + 22 = 52 6) 11 + 19 + 25 + 30 = 85 7) 37 + 13 + 40 = 90 8) 28 + 22 + 16 + 14 = 80. Reasoning: proficient if the child names the friendly pair grouped first (e.g., '23 and 17 make 40') or explains adding tens then ones. 7/8 correct = proficient.

weeks.prep: Draw bar-model mats and write word problem cards (add-to, take-from, compare, two-step). Solve Friday's 6 problems yourself first.
misconceptions: Grabbing the numbers and adding without reading. Have the child retell the story and identify whole vs. part before choosing an operation.
In two-step problems, stopping after the first step. Have the child label 'Step 1' and 'Step 2' and reread the question.

days.guide: Model drawing a bar: whole on top, parts below (or two bars for compare). Solve 6 problems, asking each time 'What do we know — the whole or the parts?'

questions.q: A class has 28 boys and 35 girls. How many children?
Ana has 32 stickers. Ben has 15 more than Ana. How many does Ben have?

days.guide: Read 'There were 45 apples. 18 were sold, then 26 more were picked.' Step 1: 45 − 18 = 27. Step 2: 27 + 26 = 53. The child labels each step.

questions.q: There were 45 apples. 18 were sold, then 26 more were picked. How many now?
Jo had 50¢, spent 20¢, then earned 15¢. How much now?

days.guide: Problem: 'Some books were on a shelf. 17 more were added. Now there are 50.' Draw a bar with ? at the start; solve 50 − 17 = 33. Check: 33 + 17 = 50.

questions.q: Some books were on a shelf. 17 more were added. Now there are 50. How many at first?
Some kids were in a pool. 12 got out. 25 are left. How many at first?

days.guide: Before solving, think 'about how much?' (e.g., 48 + 31 is about 50 + 30 = 80). Solve and check that the answer is close to the estimate.

questions.q: Estimate 48 + 31, then solve.
Someone said 62 − 19 = 81. Does that make sense?
questions.a: No — subtracting should give less than 62. The answer is 43.

days.guide: Give 6 mixed problems; each needs a bar model (or drawing) and an equation with a labeled answer.

questions.q: 72 cards. Gave 30 to Sam and 12 to Eli. How many left?
60 balloons, 24 popped. How many left?

weeks.assessment_key: Word problem set (suggested 6): 1) 45 apples, 18 sold, 26 more picked: 45 − 18 = 27, 27 + 26 = 53. 2) Ana has 32 stickers, Ben has 15 more: 47. 3) 60 balloons, 24 popped: 36. 4) Some books on a shelf, 17 added, now 50: 33. 5) 28 boys + 35 girls = 63 children. 6) 72 cards, gave 30 to Sam and 12 to Eli: 72 − 30 − 12 = 30. Rubric: 3 = correct model, equation, and labeled answer for 5–6 problems; 2 = 4 correct; 1 = 3 or fewer.

weeks.prep: Make a strategy anchor chart (blocks, number line, hundreds chart, compensation, mental) and gather digit cards 0–9. Prepare the Unit 4 test and 5 worked problems containing mistakes for Thursday.
misconceptions: In compensation, adjusting the wrong way (72 − 29 → 72 − 30 = 42, then subtract 1 = 41). Explain: you took away 1 too many, so give 1 back: 43.
Regrouping in subtraction when it isn't needed (or never). Check the ones first: 'Do I have enough ones to take away?'

days.guide: Show 39 + 26 as 40 + 25 (move 1 from 26 to 39) = 65. Show 72 − 29 as 72 − 30 = 42, then add back 1 = 43, because you subtracted 1 too many.

questions.q: Solve 39 + 26 with compensation.
Solve 72 − 29 with compensation.

days.guide: Sort 12 problems by best strategy (e.g., 50 + 30 mental; 48 + 37 number line; 99 + 24 compensation). Solve them, then discuss why each strategy fits.

questions.q: What strategy is quick for 99 + 24 and what is the answer?
Solve 50 + 30 mentally.

days.guide: Target 100: draw 4 digit cards and make two 2-digit numbers with a sum as close to 100 as possible. Record each equation and how far it is from 100. Play 8 rounds.

questions.q: With cards 4, 7, 5, 2, make two numbers whose sum is closest to 100.
How far from 100 is a sum of 104?

days.guide: Show 5 worked problems with mistakes. The child finds and fixes each and explains the error in a sentence.

questions.q: Someone wrote 46 + 38 = 74. What went wrong?
questions.a: They didn't add the regrouped ten from 14 ones; the correct answer is 84.

questions.q: Someone wrote 53 − 27 = 34. What went wrong?
questions.a: They did 7 − 3 instead of trading a ten for 13 − 7; the correct answer is 26.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test: 16 add/subtract items, multi-addend items, and 3 two-step word problems with models.

questions.q: 38 fish in a tank, 15 added, then 20 sold. How many now?

weeks.prep: Graph paper, a tally sheet with 4 fruit choices, and stickers. Line up 10–20 people to survey (family, neighbors, phone calls). Draw a new bar graph for Friday (e.g., pets: dogs 8, cats 5, fish 3, birds 6).
misconceptions: Starting the scale at 1 or using uneven spacing. Count the grid lines together from 0.
Answering 'how many more' by adding. Find both bars, then subtract the smaller from the larger.

days.guide: Make a tally sheet with 4 fruits. The child asks each person and makes tally marks, crossing every fifth mark to make a bundle. Count the totals together.

questions.q: How do you show 7 with tally marks?
questions.a: One bundle of 5 (four lines crossed by a fifth) and 2 more lines.

questions.q: Why do we bundle tallies in fives?
questions.a: Groups of 5 are quick to count.

days.guide: Make a picture graph: title, a row for each fruit, one picture per vote, and a key 'each picture = 1 vote.' Check that pictures are the same size and lined up.

questions.q: What does the key tell you?
questions.a: How many votes each picture stands for (1 vote).

questions.q: If apples got 6 votes, how many apple pictures do you draw?

days.guide: Turn the same data into a bar graph: label the axes, number the scale 0, 1, 2… evenly, and color each bar to the right height.

questions.q: Where does the scale start?
If bananas got 4 votes, how high is the bar?

days.guide: Ask questions from 2 graphs: how many in all, how many more, how many fewer. The child writes 3 questions of their own and answers them.

questions.q: Apples 7, bananas 4. How many more chose apples?
Apples 7, bananas 4, grapes 5, oranges 2. How many voted in all?

days.guide: Show the new bar graph and ask the 6 questions. The child answers each with an equation.

questions.q: Dogs 8, cats 5. How many more chose dogs?
How many votes in all (8, 5, 3, 6)?

weeks.assessment_key: Graph construction rubric: 3 = title, labeled categories and axis, scale from 0 with equal spaces, bars match data; 2 = one element missing; 1 = several missing. Quiz on the sample graph (dogs 8, cats 5, fish 3, birds 6): 1) How many chose dogs? 8 2) How many more dogs than cats? 3 3) How many fewer fish than birds? 3 4) Dogs and cats together? 13 5) How many votes in all? 22 6) If 2 more chose fish, how many fish? 5.

weeks.prep: Inch ruler, cm ruler, 15 pencils or crayons of different lengths. Prepare data for Friday's test (e.g., lengths in inches: 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7, 8; colors: red 6, blue 9, green 4, yellow 3).
misconceptions: Leaving numbers off the scale when no object has that length. Every number in the range stays on the scale, even with no X.
Confusing 'most common length' with 'longest.' Most common = tallest stack of Xs; longest = the X farthest right.

days.guide: The child measures 15 pencils or crayons to the nearest inch (starting at 0) and lists the lengths. Double-check two or three together.

questions.q: A crayon ends between 3 and 4 inches, closer to 4. What do you record?
Why start at 0 on the ruler?
questions.a: So you measure the full length.

days.guide: Draw a number line from the shortest to the longest length (e.g., 2–7 inches). Place one X above the number for each object. Add a title and the label 'Length in inches.'

questions.q: Lengths 3, 4, 4, 5. How many Xs go above 4?
If no object is 6 inches, do you still write 6 on the line?
questions.a: Yes — write 6 with no X above it.

days.guide: Measure family hand spans (thumb tip to pinky tip, hand stretched) in centimeters and make a second line plot with a cm scale.

questions.q: Spans 15, 17, 17, 18, 20 cm. Which length is most common?
What is the difference between the longest and shortest?

days.guide: Ask: most common length, longest, shortest, and the difference. The child answers in full sentences.

questions.q: Lengths 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 7. Which is most common?
What is the difference between the longest and shortest?

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test: a line plot from given measurements and a bar graph from given data, then 6 questions.

questions.q: How many Xs for 10 measurements?
Red 6, blue 9. How many more blue?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test (suggested data 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7, 8 inches): line plot with scale 3–8 and Xs: 3(1), 4(2), 5(3), 6(1), 7(2), 8(1). 1) Most common length: 5 inches. 2) Longest: 8 in. 3) Shortest: 3 in. 4) Longest − shortest: 5 in. 5) How many objects are 6 inches or longer? 4. Bar graph (red 6, blue 9, green 4, yellow 3): 6) How many more blue than green? 5. Construction rubric: title, labeled scale with equal spacing, all data shown.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks (at least 9 flats, or paper flats) and a place-value mat. Write 10 quiz problems for Friday.
misconceptions: Forgetting to add the traded ten or hundred. Write a small 1 above the next column, or use partial sums so nothing is lost.
Misaligning digits (adding 247 + 36 as if 36 were 360). Line up ones under ones in a place-value chart.

days.guide: Build 324 and 153; combine hundreds (4), tens (7), ones (7): 477. The child draws quick pictures for 8 problems without regrouping.
Build 247 + 136: ones 7 + 6 = 13, so trade 10 ones for a ten. Tens 4 + 3 + 1 = 8, hundreds 3: 383. Record with partial sums too: 300 + 70 + 13 = 383.
Build 365 + 182: tens 6 + 8 = 14 tens, so trade 10 tens for 1 hundred. Hundreds 3 + 1 + 1 = 5, tens 4, ones 7: 547. The child explains the trade aloud.

questions.q: 365 + 182 = ? What did you trade?

days.guide: Show partial sums: 365 + 182 → 300 + 100 = 400, 60 + 80 = 140, 5 + 2 = 7; 400 + 140 + 7 = 547. Match each to a block drawing for 8 problems.

questions.q: Use partial sums for 156 + 268.
Use partial sums for 509 + 237.

days.guide: Give the 10-problem quiz and ask the child to explain one regrouping step in words.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks and place-value mat. Write 10 quiz problems for Friday, including two with zeros.
misconceptions: Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column (462 − 128 = 346). Check the ones first: 2 − 8 can't be done, so trade a ten: 334.
Across zeros (400 − 165): trying to borrow from 0 tens. Trade a hundred for 10 tens first, then a ten for 10 ones — or count up instead.

days.guide: Build 586 and remove 2 hundreds, 4 tens, 3 ones: 343. The child solves 8 problems without decomposing, crossing out in quick pictures.
Build 462: you can't take 8 ones from 2, so break a ten into 10 ones (5 tens 12 ones). 12 − 8 = 4 ones, 5 − 2 = 3 tens, 4 − 1 = 3 hundreds: 334.
531 − 274: break a ten (2 tens 11 ones; 11 − 4 = 7), then break a hundred (4 hundreds 12 tens; 12 − 7 = 5 tens), then 4 − 2 = 2 hundreds: 257. The child explains each trade.
400 − 165 with blocks: trade 1 hundred for 10 tens, then 1 ten for 10 ones (3 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones): 235. Compare counting up: 165 → 200 (+35) → 400 (+200) = 235.
Give the 10-problem quiz; the child checks 3 answers by adding.

weeks.prep: Number cards, open number line paper, hundreds flats, and a timer. Write 30 quick '+/− 10 or 100' oral items and a Friday quiz.
misconceptions: Changing the ones digit when adding 10. Ask which digit is in the tens place and change only that digit (unless it crosses a hundred).
Crossing hundreds incorrectly (395 + 10 = 3105 or 305). Use blocks: 9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens = 1 hundred, so 405.

days.guide: Draw a number path for 10 numbers: write 10 less/10 more and 100 less/100 more around each. Ask which digit changes each time.

questions.q: What is 10 more and 100 more than 572?
Which digit changes when you subtract 100 from 845?

days.guide: Solve 345 + 230 on an open number line: 345 + 200 = 545, + 30 = 575. The child solves 6 more, labeling the jumps.
Call out 30 quick '+10, −10, +100, −100' items while timing. Record the time and number correct; aim to beat it next time.
Solve chains: 472 → +100 → 572 → −10 → 562. The child creates 2 chain puzzles for a family member.
Give the 15 mental items and 4 number-line problems.

questions.q: 680 − 250 on a number line?

weeks.prep: Word problem cards (within 1,000), base-ten blocks, and two dice. Prepare the Unit 6 test.
misconceptions: Rounding incorrectly for estimates (rounding 438 to 500). Find the two nearby hundreds on a number line: 438 is closer to 400.
In Race to 1,000, overshooting. Plan ahead: 'How much more do I need?'

days.guide: Read each story; the child draws quick pictures or a bar model and writes an equation. Discuss whether to add or subtract.

questions.q: A library had 425 books and got 138 more. How many now?
A school had 600 pencils and used 245. How many are left?

days.guide: Show rounding to the nearest hundred on a number line (438 is closer to 400 than 500). Estimate first, then solve and compare.

questions.q: Estimate 438 + 271 to the nearest hundred, then solve.
Estimate 812 − 389, then solve.

days.guide: The child writes a step-by-step explanation of 563 − 287 using the words hundreds, tens, ones, and trade.

questions.q: In 563 − 287, why do we break a ten first?
questions.a: 3 ones is not enough to take away 7, so trade 1 ten for 10 ones (13 ones).

days.guide: Race to 1,000: roll dice to build numbers and add them to a running total until reaching exactly 1,000. Record each equation.

questions.q: Your total is 870. How much more to reach 1,000?
Your total is 455 and you add 236. New total?

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test, including mental items and one written explanation.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test (suggested 14): 1) 425 + 138 = 563 2) 563 − 287 = 276 3) 609 + 245 = 854 4) 800 − 372 = 428 5) 136 + 247 = 383 6) 715 − 408 = 307 7) 382 + 418 = 800 8) 654 − 199 = 455 9) 250 + 375 = 625 10) 900 − 125 = 775 11) 147 + 263 = 410 12) 432 − 156 = 276 13) 508 + 92 = 600 14) 1,000 − 600 = 400. Mental: 10 more than 795 = 805; 100 less than 306 = 206. Written explanation rubric for 563 − 287: 3 = uses hundreds/tens/ones words and shows trades correctly (answer 276); 2 = correct answer with partial explanation; 1 = incorrect. Proficient: 12/14 plus a level-3 explanation.

weeks.prep: Real or play coins (pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters) and a coin purse or cup. Price pretend-store items under $1.
misconceptions: Thinking a nickel is worth more than a dime because it is bigger. Value is not size: a dime is 10¢, a nickel 5¢.
Counting each coin as 1. Sort coins first, then skip-count by each coin's value, starting with the greatest.

days.guide: Sort coins and name them: penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢. Skip-count a row of dimes by 10s and a row of nickels by 5s.

questions.q: Which is worth more: a nickel or a dime?
questions.a: A dime (10¢), even though it is smaller.

questions.q: How much are 6 dimes?

days.guide: Count mixed coins starting with the greatest value: quarter 25, dime 35, nickel 40, penny 41. Count 10 handfuls and record.

questions.q: Count: 1 quarter, 1 dime, 1 nickel, 1 penny.
Count: 2 quarters, 2 dimes, 1 penny.

days.guide: Show 50¢ four ways (2 quarters; 5 dimes; 1 quarter, 2 dimes, 1 nickel; 10 nickels) and draw each.

questions.q: Show 50¢ with quarters only.
Show 50¢ with 1 quarter plus dimes and nickels.

days.guide: Run a pretend store; the child pays exact change for items under $1 and records each purchase as coins and total cents.

questions.q: An apple costs 37¢. Which coins pay exactly?
A toy costs 85¢. Show it with quarters and a dime.

days.guide: Give the coin-counting quiz (8 collections) and 3 word problems.

questions.q: Jo has 2 dimes and 3 nickels. How many cents?
Mia has 60¢ and spends 25¢. How much is left?

weeks.assessment_key: Coin quiz (suggested 8): 1) 3 dimes = 30¢ 2) 2 quarters, 1 dime = 60¢ 3) 1 quarter, 2 nickels, 3 pennies = 38¢ 4) 4 nickels = 20¢ 5) 3 quarters = 75¢ 6) 1 quarter, 1 dime, 1 nickel, 1 penny = 41¢ 7) 5 dimes, 2 pennies = 52¢ 8) 2 dimes, 3 nickels = 35¢. Word problems: a) Jo has 2 dimes and 3 nickels → 35¢. b) A pencil costs 45¢; Sam pays with 2 quarters → 5¢ change. c) Mia has 60¢ and spends 25¢ → 35¢ left. Proficient: 10/11.

weeks.prep: Play bills ($1, $5, $10, $20) and coins, price tags, and a pretend catalog (cut from ads) with whole-dollar prices.
misconceptions: Writing both symbols ($0.65¢) or mixing them up. Teach: cents → ¢ after the number (65¢); dollars → $ before the number ($5).
Making change by guessing. Teach counting up from the price to $1 with coins.

days.guide: Show $1, $5, $10, $20 bills; count mixed bills starting with the largest. Show that 100 pennies (or 4 quarters, or 10 dimes) = $1.

questions.q: Count: one $20, one $5, two $1.
How many cents equal $1?

days.guide: Solve 6 problems with coins and bills. The child writes ¢ or $ correctly in each answer.

questions.q: Jo has 2 dimes and 3 nickels. How many cents?
Sam has a $5 bill and a $10 bill. How much money?

days.guide: Pay $1 for a 65¢ item and count up: 65 → 75 (dime) → 100 (quarter) = 35¢ change. Repeat for 80¢ and 42¢.

questions.q: An item costs 80¢. You pay $1. What is your change?
An item costs 42¢. You pay $1. What is your change?

days.guide: Choose catalog items totaling under $20 and show the addition. Ask how much money would be left.

questions.q: Items cost $7, $5, and $6. Total? Is it under $20?
Can you buy a $9 item and a $12 item with $20?

days.guide: Give 8 money word problems; check the symbols.

questions.q: You have $20 and spend $7. How much is left?
3 quarters and 1 dime?

weeks.assessment_key: Money quiz (suggested 8): 1) 2 dimes + 3 nickels = 35¢ 2) $5 + $10 + $1 = $16 3) Pay $1 for a 65¢ item → 35¢ change 4) 80¢ item from $1 → 20¢ 5) 42¢ item from $1 → 58¢ 6) $20 − $7 = $13 7) 3 quarters + 1 dime = 85¢ 8) Pencils cost 30¢ each; buy 3 → 90¢. Proficient: 7/8 with symbols used correctly.

weeks.prep: Paper plate, brass fastener, card stock for hands, markers, and an analog clock. Write 12 clock times to show on Tuesday.
misconceptions: Reading the hour hand as the next hour when it is almost there (2:50 read as 3:50). The hour hand hasn't reached 3 yet, so it is still 2 o'clock-something.
Reading the number the minute hand points to as the minutes (pointing to 5 → '5 minutes'). Count by 5s around the clock: 5 means 25 minutes.

days.guide: Make a paper-plate clock: write 1–12, then the minutes 0, 5, 10 … 55 in a ring outside the numbers. Attach a short hour hand and a long minute hand.

questions.q: When the minute hand points to 6, how many minutes?
Which hand is shorter?

days.guide: Show 12 times on the paper clock (3:25, 7:50…). The child reads the hour hand first, then counts by 5s for minutes, and matches analog to digital.

questions.q: The hour hand is between 3 and 4, and the minute hand is on 5. What time is it?
Show 7:50: where are the hands?
questions.a: Hour hand almost to 8; minute hand on 10.

days.guide: Explain: a.m. = midnight to noon, p.m. = noon to midnight. The child sorts activities and makes a daily schedule with clock drawings.

questions.q: Is breakfast usually a.m. or p.m.?
Is 7:00 bedtime a.m. or p.m.?

days.guide: Teach half past (:30), quarter past (:15), and quarter to (:45 — 15 minutes before the next hour). Check the house clock 5 times today.

questions.q: What time is quarter to 11?
What is half past 4?

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test: 10 times, a.m./p.m. choices, and 6 money problems.

questions.q: The minute hand is on 9 and the hour hand is between 6 and 7. What time?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test (suggested): Times — 1) 3:25 2) 7:50 3) 12:05 4) 9:15 (quarter past 9) 5) 4:30 (half past 4) 6) 10:45 (quarter to 11) 7) 6:10 8) 1:55 9) 8:35 10) 11:20. a.m./p.m.: breakfast a.m.; dinner p.m.; bedtime 8:00 at night p.m.; 10:00 in the morning a.m. Money: a) 3 dimes + 2 nickels = 40¢ b) $1 − 55¢ = 45¢ c) $10 + $5 + $1 = $16 d) 2 quarters + 3 pennies = 53¢ e) $20 − $8 = $12 f) 4 dimes + 1 quarter = 65¢. Proficient: 17/20.

weeks.prep: Measuring tape and a roll of adding-machine tape (or taped-together paper strips) and markers. Prepare 4 partly labeled number lines and 6 problems for Friday.
misconceptions: Counting tick marks instead of spaces (jumps). Each jump is the distance between marks; start at 0 with no jump counted yet.
Assuming every number line counts by 1. Look at two labeled marks and find the jump size first.

days.guide: Lay the measuring tape beside a number line: both start at 0 with equal spaces. On adding-machine tape, mark 0–100 with tick marks every 5 and label them.

questions.q: How is a number line like a ruler?
questions.a: Both start at 0 and have equal spaces between numbers.

questions.q: If marks go by 5s, what comes after 35?

days.guide: Show 35 as a length from 0 to 35. Then jump +20 to 55, and from 35 jump −12 to 23.

questions.q: Show 35 + 20.
questions.a: Start at 35, jump 20 to land on 55.

questions.q: Show 35 − 12.
questions.a: Start at 35, jump back 10 to 25, back 2 more to 23.

days.guide: Fill missing numbers on number lines counting by 2s, 5s, and 10s; find the jump size first.
Solve 8 problems on open number lines, labeling jumps.

questions.q: 48 + 25 on a number line.
90 − 34 on a number line.

days.guide: Give the quiz: label 4 number lines and solve 6 problems with jumps.

weeks.assessment_key: Number line quiz (suggested): label missing numbers — 1) 0, 5, __, 15, __ → 10, 20 2) 40, 50, __, 70 → 60 3) 12, 14, __, 18 → 16 4) 75, 80, __, 90 → 85. Problems on number lines: a) 35 + 20 = 55 b) 35 − 12 = 23 c) 48 + 25 = 73 d) 90 − 34 = 56 e) 27 + 46 = 73 f) 63 − 28 = 35. Proficient: 9/10 with jumps shown.

weeks.prep: Rulers, yardstick or tape, string, yarn, scissors. Choose a small rectangle (table or rug) for Tuesday. Prepare 8 length word problems for Friday.
misconceptions: Adding only two sides to find the distance around a rectangle. Walk a finger around all 4 sides and add all 4.
Mixing units in one problem. Underline the units and keep them the same.

days.guide: Read each length story, draw a bar or number line, and write an equation with units.

questions.q: A ribbon is 45 cm. 18 cm is cut off. How long is it now?
Ropes of 36 in and 25 in are tied end to end. Total length?

days.guide: Measure each side of a table or rug and add all 4 sides to find the distance around.

questions.q: A table is 40 in long and 25 in wide. What is the distance around?
How many sides do you add for a rectangle?

days.guide: Each family member does a standing long jump; measure from the start line to the back of the nearest heel. Write compare problems.

questions.q: Lia jumped 52 in and Max jumped 39 in. How much farther did Lia jump?
Where do you measure a jump to?
questions.a: From the start line to the back of the heel closest to the line.

days.guide: Solve 4 two-step length problems with number lines.

questions.q: A string is 80 cm. Two 25 cm pieces are cut off. How much is left?
One board is 30 in. Another is 20 in longer. How long are both together?

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test: 8 length word problems with number lines and equations.

questions.q: A path is 50 m; you walked 32 m. How far is left?
A snake is 28 cm and grows 9 cm. How long now?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test (suggested 8): 1) Ribbon 45 cm, 18 cm cut off → 27 cm 2) Ropes 36 in + 25 in → 61 in 3) Lia jumped 52 in, Max 39 in → 13 in farther 4) Fence sides 20, 15, 20, 15 ft → 70 ft 5) String 80 cm, two 25 cm pieces cut → 30 cm left 6) Board 64 in, need 100 in → 36 in more 7) Snake 28 cm grows 9 cm → 37 cm 8) Path 50 m, walked 32 m → 18 m left. Each needs a number line or equation. Proficient: 7/8.

weeks.prep: Counters (20), a basket of socks or shoes, hundreds chart, crayons, linking cubes.
misconceptions: Deciding odd/even from the tens digit (thinking 32 is odd). Only the ones digit decides.
Thinking 0 is neither odd nor even. 0 has no leftover, so it is even.

days.guide: Pair up counters or socks for numbers 1–20. If every item has a partner, the number is even; one left over means odd. Record in a two-column chart.

questions.q: Is 9 odd or even? How do you know?
Is 12 odd or even?

days.guide: Write each even number to 20 as a double (12 = 6 + 6) and build it with two equal cube towers.

questions.q: Write 14 as two equal addends.
Write 18 as two equal addends.

days.guide: Color the even numbers on a hundreds chart and look at the ones digits (0, 2, 4, 6, 8). Predict 47 and 86.

questions.q: Is 47 odd or even?
Is 86 odd or even?

days.guide: Test even + even, odd + odd, and even + odd with 10 examples each. The child writes the rules.

questions.q: What is odd + odd?
What is even + odd?

days.guide: Give the quiz: classify 15 numbers or groups and write 5 even numbers as equal addends.

questions.q: Is 0 odd or even?
Write 20 as equal addends.

weeks.assessment_key: Odd/even quiz (suggested 15): 7 odd, 12 even, 15 odd, 20 even, 9 odd, 14 even, 47 odd, 86 even, 33 odd, 18 even, 101 odd, 56 even, a group of 11 counters odd, a group of 16 counters even, 0 even. Equal addends: 8 = 4 + 4; 10 = 5 + 5; 14 = 7 + 7; 18 = 9 + 9; 20 = 10 + 10. Proficient: 18/20.

weeks.prep: Counters, an egg carton, a muffin tin, grid paper. Prepare 8 array pictures and 4 equations for Friday.
misconceptions: Adding the number of rows and columns (a 3-by-4 array counted as 3 + 4 = 7). Count the objects: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
Making rows of unequal length. In an array, every row has the same number.

days.guide: Make 4 groups of 3 counters. Write 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. Repeat with other equal groups.

questions.q: 4 groups of 3: repeated addition and total?
5 groups of 2?

days.guide: Find arrays at home (egg carton: 2 rows of 6; muffin tin: 3 rows of 4). Write repeated addition by rows and by columns.

questions.q: An egg carton has 2 rows of 6. Repeated addition?
A muffin tin has 3 rows of 4. Total?

days.guide: Build arrays up to 5 by 5 and draw them on grid paper. Write two equations for each (by rows and by columns).

questions.q: 3 rows with 5 in each row: two equations?
How many in 4 rows of 4?

days.guide: Solve 6 array stories with drawings and repeated addition.

questions.q: There are 4 rows of chairs with 5 chairs each. How many chairs?
3 rows of 3 cookies. How many cookies?

days.guide: Give the quiz: repeated addition for 8 arrays and draw arrays for 4 equations.

questions.q: Draw an array for 4 + 4.
5 rows of 5?

weeks.assessment_key: Array quiz (suggested): 1) 2 rows of 5 → 5 + 5 = 10 2) 3 rows of 4 → 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 3) 4 rows of 3 → 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 4) 5 rows of 2 → 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10 5) 3 rows of 5 → 15 6) 4 rows of 4 → 16 7) 5 rows of 5 → 25 8) 2 rows of 3 → 6. Draw: a) 3 + 3 + 3 → 3 rows of 3 b) 4 + 4 → 2 rows of 4 c) 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 → 4 rows of 5 d) 2 + 2 + 2 → 3 rows of 2. Proficient: 11/12.

weeks.prep: Grid paper, square tiles or square crackers. Prepare the 12-item Unit 9 test.
misconceptions: Thinking 2 rows of 6 and 6 rows of 2 have different totals. Turn the array to show it's the same 12.
Guessing odd/even from the row size (3 rows of 4 = 12 is even). Find the total, then check the ones digit.

days.guide: Build arrays with tiles or crackers and write 10 repeated-addition equations.

questions.q: 5 rows of 3 tiles: total?
2 rows of 4 crackers?

days.guide: Design a garden with 4 rows of 5 plants (20) and other arrays. Decide whether each total is odd or even.

questions.q: 4 rows of 5 plants: total, odd or even?
3 rows of 3 plants?

days.guide: Find all rectangular arrays that make 12 using tiles.

questions.q: Find arrays that make 12.
questions.a: 1 row of 12, 2 rows of 6, 3 rows of 4 (and 4 of 3, 6 of 2, 12 of 1).

questions.q: Is 12 odd or even?

days.guide: Solve 6 mixed problems on arrays, equal groups, and odd/even.

questions.q: 3 bags with 5 apples each. Total? Odd or even?
Can 14 kids make 2 equal teams?

days.guide: Give the 12-item Unit 9 test.

questions.q: Is 22 odd or even?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test (suggested 12): 1) 15 → odd 2) 22 → even 3) 16 = 8 + 8 4) 3 rows of 4 → 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 5) 5 rows of 3 → 15 6) 2 rows of 5 → 10, even 7) draw 4 + 4 + 4 → 3 rows of 4 8) arrays for 12: 1 by 12, 2 by 6, 3 by 4 (and turned versions) 9) 4 rows of 5 trees → 20 10) 3 bags of 5 apples → 15 11) 3 rows of 5 → 15, odd 12) 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8, even. Proficient: 10/12.

weeks.prep: Geoboard or dot paper, pattern blocks (or paper cutouts), straws with clay or pipe-cleaner connectors.
misconceptions: Thinking a turned square is no longer a square ('it's a diamond'). Turn it back and count equal sides and square corners.
Thinking only the pattern-block hexagon is a hexagon. Any closed shape with 6 straight sides is a hexagon.

days.guide: Sort pattern blocks and cutouts by number of sides and angles. Name the groups: triangle (3), quadrilateral (4), pentagon (5), hexagon (6).

questions.q: How many sides does a hexagon have?
A shape has 5 angles. What is it?

days.guide: Make a square, rectangle, rhombus, and trapezoid on a geoboard. List what they share (4 sides, 4 angles).

questions.q: What do all quadrilaterals have?
How is a rhombus different from a square?
questions.a: A rhombus has 4 equal sides but does not need square corners.

days.guide: Read a clue; the child draws a shape that fits.

questions.q: Draw a quadrilateral with no square corners.
questions.a: Example: a slanted rhombus or a trapezoid with slanted sides.

questions.q: Draw a shape with 5 sides.

days.guide: Build shapes with straws and connectors; count sides and vertices (corners).

questions.q: How many vertices does a triangle have?
A shape has 4 sides. How many vertices?

days.guide: Give the 10-item attribute quiz.

questions.q: 4 equal sides and 4 square corners?
6 sides?

weeks.assessment_key: Shape quiz (suggested 10 clues): 1) 3 sides, 3 angles → triangle 2) 4 sides → quadrilateral 3) 5 sides → pentagon 4) 6 sides → hexagon 5) 4 equal sides, 4 square corners → square 6) 4 square corners, sides not all equal → rectangle 7) 4 equal sides, no square corners → rhombus 8) quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides → trapezoid 9) draw a shape with 5 sides → any closed pentagon 10) 6 vertices → hexagon. Proficient: 9/10.

weeks.prep: Dice, sugar cubes, boxes, grid paper, square tiles.
misconceptions: Counting only the faces you can see on a cube (3). Turn it to count all 6.
Drawing uneven rows when partitioning. Use grid paper to make same-size squares.

days.guide: Examine a die. Count faces (6), edges (12), and vertices (8), marking each with a sticker or pencil dot as you count.

questions.q: How many faces does a cube have?
How many edges and vertices?

days.guide: Hunt for 3-D shapes at home (cubes, boxes, cans, balls) and record which have square faces.

questions.q: Does a soup can have square faces?
questions.a: No — its flat faces are circles.

questions.q: Does every box have square faces?
questions.a: No — many boxes have rectangle faces; only a cube-shaped box has all square faces.

days.guide: Cover a rectangle with square tiles, no gaps or overlaps; draw lines for rows and columns and count.

questions.q: A rectangle is covered by 2 rows of 5 tiles. How many tiles?
Why no gaps or overlaps?
questions.a: So every part is covered exactly once and the count is correct.

days.guide: Partition rectangles into 2 rows of 4, 3 rows of 3, etc. on paper and connect to repeated addition.

questions.q: 3 rows of 3 squares: total and addition?
2 rows of 4?

days.guide: Give the quiz on cube attributes and 6 partitioning problems.

questions.q: 4 rows of 4 squares: total?
How many vertices on a cube?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested): cube — 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices, every face a square. Partition-and-count: 1) 2 rows of 4 → 8 squares 2) 3 rows of 3 → 9 3) 2 rows of 5 → 10 4) 4 rows of 2 → 8 5) 3 rows of 5 → 15 6) 4 rows of 4 → 16. Proficient: 8/9.

weeks.prep: Paper circles and rectangles, scissors, play dough, crackers or tortillas.
misconceptions: Calling any 2 pieces 'halves.' Halves must be equal in size.
Thinking equal shares must look the same. Show fourths of a square as 4 small squares and as 4 triangles — each is still one-fourth.

days.guide: Fold paper rectangles and circles in half different ways (lengthwise, crosswise, diagonally). Decide which folds make equal shares.

questions.q: Is a rectangle cut into 2 unequal pieces cut into halves?
How many halves make a whole?

days.guide: Cut play-dough pizzas and paper rectangles into thirds and fourths; label each piece.

questions.q: How many thirds make a whole?
If a pizza is cut into 4 equal pieces, what is each piece called?

days.guide: Cut 3 identical squares into fourths different ways (4 small squares, 4 strips, 4 triangles). Explain why each piece is still a fourth.

questions.q: A square cut into 4 triangles and another into 4 small squares: are all the pieces fourths?
questions.a: Yes — each is 1 of 4 equal parts of the same-size whole.

questions.q: Do equal shares need to be the same shape?

days.guide: Share a tortilla or sandwich equally among 2, 3, or 4 people and describe the shares.

questions.q: If 3 people share a tortilla equally, what does each get?
More people sharing the same tortilla: bigger or smaller pieces?

days.guide: Give the Unit 10 test.

questions.q: Shade half of a rectangle.
How many fourths make a whole?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 10 test (suggested 12): 1) 3 sides → triangle 2) 6 sides → hexagon 3) 4 sides → quadrilateral 4) 5 sides → pentagon 5) rectangle in 2 rows of 3 → 6 squares 6) 3 rows of 4 → 12 squares 7) shade half of a circle (1 of 2 equal parts) 8) show thirds of a rectangle (3 equal parts) 9) show fourths of a square (4 equal parts) 10) choose the picture with equal shares (equal-size parts) 11) a pizza cut into 4 equal pieces: each is a fourth 12) 2 halves make a whole. Proficient: 10/12.

weeks.prep: Fact cards, base-ten blocks, and the fluency graph from Weeks 1 and 4. Write 12 within-100 and 10 within-1,000 problems.
misconceptions: Rushing facts and making careless errors. Focus on accuracy first, then speed.
Choosing the wrong operation in two-step problems. Have the child explain what each step finds.

days.guide: Give the 40-fact quiz and graph the score next to the baseline. Talk about the growth.
Solve 12 mixed problems within 100; the child explains one strategy aloud.
Solve 10 mixed problems within 1,000, drawing quick pictures where needed.
Solve 4 two-step stories and write one of your own.

questions.q: 120 stickers. Gave away 35, bought 50. How many now?
A farm had 200 eggs, sold 75, then collected 40. How many now?

days.guide: Complete a self-check (place value, fact families, regrouping) and mark two topics to practice next week.

questions.q: What is the value of the 6 in 562?
Write the fact family for 5, 8, 13.

weeks.assessment_key: Fluency quiz: score out of 40, graphed beside earlier scores (growth expected; 36+ shows mastery). Mixed problems (suggested): 54 + 29 = 83; 81 − 37 = 44; 345 + 278 = 623; 702 − 456 = 246; two-step: 120 stickers, gave away 35, bought 50 → 135. Proficient: about 85% correct and a clear explanation.

weeks.prep: Rulers, coins, a clock, graph paper. Prepare 15 mixed review items for Friday.
misconceptions: Measuring from 1 instead of 0. Check the starting point every time.
Counting coins in random order. Sort from greatest to least value first.

days.guide: Measure 5 objects in inches and cm; solve 2 compare-length problems.

questions.q: A pencil is 15 cm and a crayon is 9 cm. How much longer is the pencil?
For the same pencil, which number is bigger: inches or cm?

days.guide: Count coin sets and tell time at 6 moments today; solve 3 money problems.

questions.q: 2 quarters and 1 dime?
The minute hand is on 3 and the hour hand just past 2. Time?

days.guide: Survey family about favorite summer activity, make a bar graph, and write 3 questions about it.

questions.q: Swim 6, bike 4. How many more chose swim?
What must a bar graph have?
questions.a: A title, labels, and a scale starting at 0 with equal spaces.

days.guide: Draw shapes from clues and partition shapes into equal shares.

questions.q: Draw a shape with 4 sides and 4 square corners.
Divide a circle into thirds.

days.guide: Give 15 mixed items across measurement, data, and geometry.

questions.q: How many faces on a cube?

weeks.assessment_key: Mixed review (suggested 15): 1) measure a 6 cm line → 6 cm 2) measure a 3 in line → 3 in 3) 12 in − 8 in = 4 in 4) 2 quarters + 1 dime = 60¢ 5) $1 − 35¢ = 65¢ 6) clock showing 4:45 → 4:45 / quarter to 5 7) bar graph: 9 − 5 = 4 more 8) line plot: most common value is the tallest stack 9) triangle → 3 sides 10) hexagon → 6 sides 11) cube → 6 faces 12) halves → 2 equal parts 13) 3 rows of 4 → 12 14) fourths of a circle → 4 equal parts 15) 25 cm + 30 cm = 55 cm. Proficient: 13/15.

weeks.prep: Print or write the year-end test (two parts), poster board, markers, glue, and photos or drawing paper.
misconceptions: Getting stuck and leaving the rest blank. Remind the child to do what they know first, then return.
Posters with pictures but no math. Each picture needs a label with numbers and an equation.

days.guide: Give part 1 of the year-end test. Read instructions aloud but not answers.
Give part 2: measurement, graphs, money, time, shapes, and equal shares.

questions.q: 3 quarters + 2 dimes?
The minute hand is on 7 and the hour hand is past 8. Time?

days.guide: Plan a 'Math in My Home' poster with an array (egg carton), a measurement (a table), money (a price), and a graph.

questions.q: What array could you show from home?
questions.a: Example: an egg carton with 2 rows of 6 = 12.

questions.q: Name one measurement you could add.
questions.a: Example: the kitchen table is 48 inches long.

days.guide: Finish the poster with labeled pictures and practice explaining each idea aloud in about 3 minutes.

questions.q: Explain your array.
questions.a: Example: 'This muffin tin has 3 rows of 4, so 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 cups.'

questions.q: Why label pictures with numbers?
questions.a: So people can see the math in each picture.

days.guide: The child presents the poster to family; review the fluency growth graph from the year together.

questions.q: How did your fluency scores change this year?
questions.a: Answer from the graph — scores should rise from the Week 1 baseline.

questions.q: What math idea are you most proud of?
questions.a: Any specific answer with an example.

weeks.assessment_key: Year-end test part 1 (suggested): 1) 467 = 400 + 60 + 7 2) 528 < 582 3) 58 + 37 = 95 4) 90 − 46 = 44 5) 356 + 278 = 634 6) 600 − 245 = 355 7) 45 stickers, gave away 18, got 20 more → 47. Part 2: 8) measure lines (accept ±1 unit) 9) answer graph questions from the given bar graph and line plot 10) 3 quarters + 2 dimes = 95¢ 11) clock reading 8:35 12) 5 sides → pentagon 13) shade one fourth. Math fair rubric: 4 = arrays, a measurement, money, and a graph each shown with correct numbers and clearly explained in about 3 minutes; 3 = all shown, minor errors; 2 = 2–3 ideas; 1 = 1 idea.
